newsitem.title: USA: House panel kills bid to preserve ethanol tax break.
newsitem.headline: House panel kills bid to preserve ethanol tax break.

text.p: In a blow to farmers and agriculture groups, the House tax-writing panel Thursday narrowly defeated a measure to preserve the ethanol tax break, worth billions of dollars a year to American farmers.
The House Ways and Means Committee voted 21 to 17 against an amendment that would have retained the tax subsidies for the corn-based fuel by cutting back on corporate capital gains tax relief.

"There is only one ultimate answer and that is the free market economy," committee Chairman Bill Archer said of the ethanol subsidies. "This distorts that." The Texas Republican said companies have sold farmers "a bill of goods" that ethanol production is the only way to make a profit.
"It is leading farmers into a dead alley," Archer said. "The highest and best use of corn is to feed human beings."
The amendment was offered by Representatives Jim Nussle, Iowa Republican, and John Tanner, a Tennessee Democrat.

Lawmakers were expected to vote later Thursday on other amendments on Archer's plan to phase out ethanol subsidies. Ethanol backers are worried if the plan goes forward from the tax panel it will be more difficult to defeat.
"It will be a bad sign if it gets out of committee," said Dave Lane of the American Farm Bureau. "We haven't felt the support for it. It's more of a cornbelt issue than a national issue."

Currently, oil companies get a tax credit of 5.4 cents per gallon when they blend ethanol with gasoline. Archer has proposed paring the tax break about a third of a cent and eliminating it in the year 2000.

His plan faces stiff opposition from cornbelt lawmakers, farm groups and the Clinton administration, who all say ethanol is a clean-burning fuel that spurs economic growth in rural America. They say Congress must make good on its promise to keep the tax break in place until the year 2000.
The ethanol tax credit is worth billions of dollars a year to farmers. Ethanol, an alcohol-based fuel derived from corn and other grains, accounts for 5 percent of corn demand.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin served notice on Wednesday that the White House would fight efforts to scale back the ethanol tax break. The administration favors extending the subsidy passed the year 2000.

A bipartisan group of farm state senators said Thursday they were ready for "an all-out battle" if anti-ethanol legislation came up in the Senate. Last month, 100 House members urged congressional leaders to protect the tax incentive.
